title: Logic and Critical Thinking
tagline: The structure of arguments, concepts and definition, propositions, deductive reasoning, the syllogism, induction and analogy, causal reasoning, fallacies, evaluating information, and logic in ancient China
summary: Clear writing depends on clear thinking. This course introduces the logic taught in Chinese universities — concepts and definitions, propositions, deductive inference and the syllogism, induction, analogy and causal reasoning — together with the practical skills of critical thinking: recognising fallacies, weighing evidence and judging the claims met in the news and online. It ends with the logical traditions of ancient China.
overview: A first course in logic for writers: not a tour of formal systems, but the workshop manual of reasoning—how arguments are built, how they fail, and how to tell the difference in the wild.

It moves from the anatomy of an argument through definition, proposition, deduction, syllogism, induction, causation and fallacy, to the practical logic of evaluating information and the classical Chinese traditions of ming-bian and lian-bai.
Every technique is drilled on Chinese-language material: exam essays, editorials, ad copy, chat screenshots—logic is taught as a reading device for the texts students actually meet.
outcomes: Reconstruct arguments into premise–conclusion form and separate inference from persuasion
Test definitions against the four classical rules and repair faulty ones
Distinguish valid from sound, and use truth-functional connectives correctly
Evaluate syllogisms with classical rules and simple diagramming; recognise the figures that fail
Assess induction, analogy and causal claims (Mill's methods, confounders, base rates)
Diagnose the standard fallacies by name and by repair, in authentic Chinese media texts
Apply evidential standards (source, sample, independence, relevance) to everyday information
Read Mohist and Ming-era logical texts as contributions to argument theory, not curiosities

chapters.title: The structure of arguments
chapters.summary: Premises and conclusions, finding the argument in a text, and validity and soundness.

chapters.title: Concepts and definition
chapters.summary: Intension and extension, relations between concepts, definition and division, and their common errors.

chapters.title: Propositions
chapters.summary: Simple and compound propositions — negation, conjunction, disjunction and conditionals — and the square of opposition.

chapters.title: Deductive reasoning
chapters.summary: Inferences from compound propositions, conditional reasoning, and dilemmas.

chapters.title: The syllogism
chapters.summary: Categorical syllogisms, their rules and figures, and checking them with diagrams.

chapters.title: Induction and analogy
chapters.summary: Induction by enumeration, statistical generalisation and analogy, and how strong each can be.

chapters.title: Causal reasoning
chapters.summary: Mill’s methods, correlation and causation, and confounding factors.

chapters.title: Fallacies
chapters.summary: Equivocation, begging the question, false dilemma, slippery slope, personal attack, appeals to authority and to the crowd, and the straw man.

chapters.title: Evaluating information
chapters.summary: Sources, statistics and rumours, checking claims met online, and reflecting on one’s own biases.

chapters.title: Logic in ancient China
chapters.summary: The logic of the Mohist canons, Gongsun Long and the School of Names, and Xunzi on the rectification of names.

history.title: Aristotle founds the syllogistic
history.detail: The Prior Analytics analyses deduction through figure and mood: the first formal science of inference.

history.title: The Mohist Canon of disputation
history.detail: The Xiao Qu and Da Qu chapters systematise cu, le, shuo and yan—Chinese induction, analogy, explanation and exemplum.

history.title: The white horse is not a horse
history.detail: Gongsun Long's paradoxes separate name from object and thing from attribute; the School of Names at work.

history.title: An algebra of thought
history.detail: Boole's Laws of Thought renders logic as calculation with 0, 1 and classes—foundation of the digital age.

history.title: The concept-script
history.detail: Frege's Begriffsschrift creates quantifiers and function–argument analysis: modern logic begins.

history.title: Principia Mathematica
history.detail: Russell and Whitehead attempt to derive mathematics from logic; type theory tames the paradoxes.

history.title: Logic and native thought
history.detail: Jin Yuelin's treatise situates the ancient Chinese schools—ming-bian, lian-bai, the Canon—in comparative logic.

history.title: The logic textbook generation
history.detail: Copi's symbolic course settles the modern intro syllabus; the informal-logic movement then returns argument to essays and newsrooms.
